title: Media professionals are drifting away from the public they model: platform overestimation coexists with advertising distrust and shared-screen attachment
geography: Canada; adults aged 18-59 and Canadian Marketing Association media/advertising professionals

observations.period: July-August 2026; public media use versus industry estimates

denominator.unit: Canadians aged 18-59 who do not work in marketing or media, surveyed through an Ipsos online panel

tiktok_actual_use.unit: percent of Canadian respondents reporting TikTok use in the past month

tiktok_industry_estimate.unit: percent estimated by media/advertising professionals as public TikTok use in the past month

estimation_gap.unit: percentage-point difference between reported public use and industry estimate

modeling_distance.value: The audience that media systems model can become a professional projection rather than an observed public.

observations.method: Two-sample cross-sectional study: 600 Canadian adults aged 18-59 outside marketing/media industries and 174 Canadian Marketing Association members in advertising, publishing, media, creative, or digital agencies.
observations.uncertainty: The public sample is an online Ipsos panel and the professional sample is a membership-based industry sample; the comparison is descriptive, not a causal estimate of media planning or platform adoption.
observations.subgroup: Canadian adults aged 18-59 versus Canadian marketing/media professionals; the release does not provide full weighting or demographic cross-tabs.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap may partly reflect different definitions of use, recency, audience reach, or extrapolation targets rather than simple ignorance of public behavior.

observations.period: July-August 2026; advertising trust and data/fake-content concerns

denominator.unit: Canadian adults aged 18-59 outside marketing/media industries; professional comparison sample is 174

no_advertising_trust.unit: percent of Canadians saying they do not trust any advertising today

no_advertising_trust_prior.unit: percent in the publisher's comparison a decade earlier

data_collection_concern.value: Personal-data collection and use are among Canadians' top advertising concerns.

ai_fake_content_concern.value: Misleading or fake content ranks highest among perceived risks associated with AI-generated advertising.

observations.method: Descriptive public/professional survey comparison with a decade comparison reported by the publisher.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not provide the full response distribution, question wording, weighting, or a causal decomposition of distrust; a stable topline does not imply stable reasons.
observations.subgroup: Canadian adults aged 18-59, with industry-professional contrasts where reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Advertising distrust may coexist with effective attention, recognition, or purchasing; concern about AI content may also reflect general information skepticism.

observations.period: July-August 2026; social advertising attention and consumer/industry divergence

denominator.unit: Canadian adults aged 18-59 outside marketing/media industries; professional comparison sample is 174

social_advertising_alignment.value: Canadian respondents broadly describe social advertising as misleading, low quality, or untrustworthy, while industry professionals are more likely to like it.

industry_attention_belief.value: Industry respondents are more likely than the public to say social advertising earns attention and makes people want to buy.

television_ad_attention.value: Canadians rate television highest for the reported attention and purchase-influence attributes.

translation_gap.value: A channel's professional performance narrative can diverge from the audience's felt credibility and attention experience.

observations.method: Comparative descriptive survey of Canadian consumers and media/advertising professionals.
observations.uncertainty: The public release does not provide all scale points or subgroup distributions, and stated attention or purchase influence is not observed conversion.
observations.subgroup: Canadian adults aged 18-59 versus Canadian Marketing Association professionals.
observations.counterinterpretation: Different media goals can produce different valid judgments: professionals may assess campaign performance while consumers report personal experience.

observations.period: July-August 2026; fragmented media and shared television experience

denominator.unit: Canadian adults aged 18-59 outside marketing/media industries; professional comparison sample is 174

shared_tv_value.value: Canadians continue to value live television as a distinct form of engagement and connection despite fragmented platform and device use.

fragmentation_context.value: Media consumption is increasingly distributed across platforms and devices, but fragmentation does not erase shared-screen value.

fourth_wave_persistence.value: The public/professional gap has persisted across four editions over roughly a decade.

cultural-interface_route.value: Media infrastructure is not only a delivery channel; it shapes shared attention, credibility, and the social experience of culture.

observations.method: Fourth edition of the thinkTV/Ipsos Ad Nation study; current fieldwork used separate consumer and industry samples.
observations.uncertainty: The release does not establish causal effects of television, fragmentation, or shared viewing on social cohesion, purchasing, or political behavior.
observations.subgroup: Canadian adults aged 18-59 and media/advertising professionals.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reported shared-TV value may reflect content, habit, event programming, or household composition rather than the broadcast technology itself.

related_sources.claim: The official thinkTV release provides the 2026 findings, public/professional sample sizes, fieldwork dates, platform-use gap, advertising trust, social-advertising contrasts, and shared-television interpretation.

boundary: This record adds a consumer-media translation route: professional assumptions can diverge from public behavior, while advertising trust, AI-content concern, social-ad credibility, and shared television shape cultural attention. It does not establish causal campaign performance, platform market share, purchase conversion, social cohesion, or political effects.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official thinkTV Ad Nation 2026 page was reviewed for the two-sample design, fieldwork dates, TikTok usage/estimate gap, advertising trust, data and AI-content concerns, social-advertising contrasts, television value, and repeated-study context.
